notes.front: What is a towered airport?
notes.back: An airport with an operating control tower, where air traffic control keeps traffic flowing safely and in order.
notes.explanation: Manned pilots there must keep two-way radio contact with ATC, so a remote pilot nearby can hear who is where by monitoring the tower frequency.
notes.example: Like a road junction with traffic lights: someone (the tower) decides who goes when.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65; Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, p. 14-2

notes.front: What is a non-towered airport?
notes.back: An airport without an operating control tower; two-way radio is not required, though it is good practice for pilots to monitor a common frequency.
notes.explanation: Nobody sequences the traffic, so pilots rely on seeing each other and on voluntary radio calls.
notes.example: Like a junction with no lights: drivers look, signal and give way on their own.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: What is UNICOM?
notes.back: A nongovernment air/ground radio station that may give airport information at public-use airports with no tower or Flight Service Station.
notes.explanation: At many non-towered airports the UNICOM frequency is also the CTAF, so it is often where local traffic calls are heard.
notes.example: Like the front desk of a small airfield answering pilots’ questions over the radio.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: What is MULTICOM?
notes.back: The self-announce frequency, 122.9, used at a non-towered airport that has no Flight Service Station or UNICOM.
notes.explanation: With nobody on the ground to answer, pilots simply announce their own positions and intentions on 122.9.
notes.example: Like announcing “coming through” in a corridor when there is no receptionist to direct people.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: What is a self-announce broadcast?
notes.back: A pilot’s radio call, made “in the blind” on the common frequency, stating who they are, where they are and what they intend.
notes.explanation: No one acknowledges it; it exists so other traffic, including a listening remote pilot, can picture where each aircraft is.
notes.example: “Town and Country traffic, Cessna 123 Bravo Foxtrot, left base, runway 18, Town and Country traffic.”
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: What is an aircraft call sign?
notes.back: The name an aircraft uses on the radio, usually built from its registration (“N”) number or an airline name and flight number.
notes.explanation: Recognising call signs lets a remote pilot tell which aircraft a radio call is about and what kind of aircraft it is.
notes.example: N123AB, a Cessna 172, calls itself “Cessna One-Two-Three-Alpha-Bravo”.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 42

notes.front: What is the phonetic alphabet used in aviation radio?
notes.back: The ICAO set of code words for letters (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie…) used so letters are not misheard.
notes.explanation: Pilots use it to say registration numbers and to spell words when reception is poor.
notes.example: “B” and “D” sound alike on a crackly radio; “Bravo” and “Delta” do not.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-7 “Phonetic Alphabet”

notes.front: What is an airport traffic pattern?
notes.back: The standard rectangular path aircraft fly around an airport to take off and land: upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final.
notes.explanation: Knowing where manned aircraft will be, and at what height, tells a remote pilot where not to fly near an airport.
notes.example: Like a one-way loop round a car park: everyone joins and leaves at predictable points.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-3 “Traffic Patterns”

notes.front: What is an airport beacon?
notes.back: A flashing or rotating light, normally on from dusk to dawn, whose colours show what type of airport it marks.
notes.explanation: At twilight or night a remote pilot can use it to spot an airport, and its colours say whether it is a land airport, water airport or heliport.
notes.example: Like a lighthouse whose colour pattern tells sailors which harbour it is.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Airport Beacon”, p. 14-16

notes.front: What is a VASI (visual approach slope indicator)?
notes.back: Bars of lights near a runway that show a landing pilot, by red and white colours, whether they are above, on or below the glidepath.
notes.explanation: It tells you where manned aircraft on final approach are meant to be descending.
notes.example: Like parking sensors that change colour as you get closer to the right position.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI)”, p. 14-16

notes.front: What is a PAPI (precision approach path indicator)?
notes.back: Runway lights, similar to a VASI’s, that show a landing pilot the visual glide path.
notes.explanation: Red and white lights show approaching aircraft are on the slope down to the runway, so a remote pilot near an airport can expect traffic descending along that path.
notes.example: Aircraft on final approach follow the PAPI down, so they will be descending along that path toward the runway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-1-2, “Visual Glideslope Indicators”

notes.front: What is a SIDA (Security Identification Display Area)?
notes.back: A limited-access area of an airport where you need a badge issued under 49 CFR part 1542 to enter.
notes.explanation: A remote pilot working at an airport must not enter one without authorisation and displayed identification.
notes.example: Like the “staff only” area behind airport security, where everyone wears a visible badge.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 2-3-15 “Security Identification Display Area (SIDA)”

notes.front: What is a runway holding position marking?
notes.back: Four yellow lines across a taxiway, two solid and two dashed, showing where to stop before a runway.
notes.explanation: It is the painted “stop line” before a runway; at a towered airport you cross the solid lines only with an ATC clearance.
notes.example: Like the stop line at a level crossing.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Runway Holding Position Marking”, p. 14-8

notes.front: A CTAF can be a UNICOM, MULTICOM or Flight Service Station frequency, or even a {{c1::tower}} frequency, as published for that airport.
notes.explanation: A part-time tower’s frequency can serve as the CTAF when the tower is closed; the right one is listed in aeronautical publications.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: What frequency is UNICOM usually on at a non-towered airport?
notes.back: 122.8, but check the Chart Supplement or sectional chart, because it varies.
notes.explanation: Where many non-towered airports are close together, different UNICOM frequencies are assigned, so the published one is the one to use.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: At a non-towered airport with no Flight Service Station or UNICOM, which frequency is used?
notes.back: MULTICOM, 122.9.
notes.explanation: With no frequency listed for the airport, pilots self-announce on 122.9.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: Where should a remote pilot check the correct frequency for an airport before flying nearby?
notes.back: The Chart Supplement U.S. or the sectional chart.
notes.explanation: Frequencies are printed beside the airport on the sectional chart and listed in the Chart Supplement entry.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: How far from a non-towered airport does an inbound manned pilot normally make the first self-announce call?
notes.back: About 10 miles out, giving their direction from the airport (north, south, east or west).
notes.explanation: The call “in the blind” tells everyone on the CTAF who is coming and from where.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: Why does a self-announce call name the airport at both the start and the end?
notes.back: So others on the frequency can confirm which airport the aircraft means.
notes.explanation: The Study Guide’s reason: to allow others who are on the frequency to confirm where the aircraft is going.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 41

notes.front: Arriving at a non-towered airport, a manned pilot self-announces about 10 miles out, then on entering downwind, base and final, and again on {{c1::leaving the runway}}.
notes.explanation: These recommended calls let listeners track an aircraft all the way round the pattern.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Figure 14-1. Recommended communication procedures”, p. 14-3

notes.front: Are manned pilots required by regulation to make radio calls near a non-towered airport?
notes.back: No. It is good practice, not mandatory, so a remote pilot must always look for aircraft too.
notes.explanation: A silent frequency does not mean an empty sky; the radio is only an extra layer of situational awareness.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 41

notes.front: When may a remote pilot transmit on an active aviation frequency?
notes.back: Only in an emergency; otherwise they should listen, not transmit.
notes.explanation: Remote pilots are not expected to talk to manned aircraft; monitoring is encouraged, transmitting is not.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 41

notes.front: Does part 107 require a remote pilot flying near an airport to carry an aviation radio?
notes.back: No; part 107 requires authorisation in certain airport areas, but monitoring with a radio is only good practice.
notes.explanation: Listening helps a remote pilot understand nearby manned traffic even though no radio is required.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 41

notes.front: At a towered airport, what must manned pilots maintain with ATC?
notes.back: Two-way radio communication, and they must acknowledge and comply with ATC instructions.
notes.explanation: That is why a remote pilot monitoring the tower frequency can hear where manned traffic is being sent.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Towered Airport”, p. 14-2

notes.front: At a non-towered airport, is two-way radio communication required?
notes.back: No, although it is good practice for pilots to monitor the specified common frequency.
notes.explanation: Some aircraft at non-towered airports have no radio at all, which is why looking outside matters.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: How is the registration N123AB spoken in full on the radio?
notes.back: “November One-Two-Three-Alpha-Bravo.”
notes.explanation: US-registered aircraft have “N” numbers, and letters are spoken with the phonetic alphabet.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 42

notes.front: In a light general-aviation aircraft’s call sign, what usually replaces “November”?
notes.back: The manufacturer’s name, e.g. “Cessna One-Two-Three-Alpha-Bravo”.
notes.explanation: When the make or model is stated, the “N” prefix is dropped.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 42

notes.front: In the call sign of a heavier general-aviation aircraft, such as a turboprop (a propeller turned by a jet engine) or jet, what replaces “November”?
notes.back: Usually the aircraft’s model, e.g. “Citation One-Two-Three-Alpha-Bravo”.
notes.explanation: Light aircraft usually use the make; heavier ones usually use the model.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 42

notes.front: How do airliners usually form their call sign?
notes.back: Company name plus flight number, e.g. “Southwest Seven-One-One”.
notes.explanation: A few airlines use a different word: British Airways uses “Speedbird”.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 42

notes.front: In the phonetic alphabet, what is the word for the letter A?
notes.back: Alfa.
notes.explanation: Pilots use the phonetic alphabet to identify their aircraft, so any A in a call sign is spoken as “Alfa”.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-7 “Phonetic Alphabet”; Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, pp. 40–41

notes.front: How is the digit 9 pronounced on the aviation radio?
notes.back: “Niner”.
notes.explanation: Numbers in a call sign are spoken digit by digit (e.g. “One-Two-Three”), and 9 is always said “niner”.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-7 “Phonetic Alphabet”

notes.front: Below 18,000 feet MSL, how is an altitude of 12,500 feet spoken?
notes.back: “One two thousand five hundred”: the separate digits of the thousands, plus the hundreds.
notes.explanation: At and above 18,000 feet MSL, pilots say “flight level” instead.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-9 “Altitudes and Flight Levels”

notes.front: How is 4,500 feet spoken on the radio?
notes.back: “Four thousand five hundred.”
notes.explanation: Round hundreds and thousands up to 9,900 are spoken as words; above that, the digits before “thousand” are separated (10,000 = “one zero thousand”).
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-8 “Figures”

notes.front: On the radio, are headings, courses and wind directions given as magnetic or true?
notes.back: Magnetic, as three digits; the word “true” is added when a direction is true.
notes.explanation: Written reports (METAR, TAF) give wind from true north; winds spoken by ATC or ATIS are magnetic. Heading is the way the aircraft’s nose points.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-10 “Directions”

notes.front: How is a speed of 250 knots spoken on the radio?
notes.back: “Two five zero knots”: the separate digits followed by “knots”.
notes.explanation: Controllers may drop “knots” when giving speed adjustments.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-11 “Speeds”

notes.front: What time standard does the FAA use on the radio, and how is local time marked?
notes.back: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC, “Zulu”); local time is marked with “local” or the time zone.
notes.explanation: Times are given on the 24-hour clock, e.g. 0920 is “zero niner two zero”.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-12 “Time”

notes.front: Does the definition of an airport include seaplane bases and heliports?
notes.back: Yes: an airport is any area of land or water used or intended for aircraft landing or takeoff, including seaplane bases and heliports.
notes.explanation: So a heliport or a seaplane base near your flight area counts as an airport when you plan.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: What is a private airport?
notes.back: An airport designated for private or restricted use only, not open to the general public.
notes.explanation: Airports divide into towered and non-towered, and further into civil, military/federal government and private.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: What is a civil airport?
notes.back: An airport open to the general public.
notes.explanation: Contrast military/federal airports (run by the military, NASA or other federal agencies) and private airports.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: Who operates military/federal government airports?
notes.back: The military, NASA or other federal government agencies.
notes.explanation: They are one of the three subdivisions, with civil and private airports.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: Before flying near an airport, a remote pilot can find its current data on aeronautical charts, in the Chart Supplement U.S., in NOTAMs and from {{c1::ATIS}}.
notes.explanation: These sources give frequencies, services, closed runways and construction.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 66

notes.front: Unless otherwise indicated, which way do aircraft turn in the traffic pattern?
notes.back: To the left (except helicopters, where applicable).
notes.explanation: So on a standard pattern, the downwind leg is on the left side of the runway as seen by a landing pilot.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-3 “Traffic Patterns”

notes.front: On a sectional chart, what does “RP 18” at the bottom of an airport data block mean?
notes.back: Right traffic pattern for runway 18.
notes.explanation: Right patterns are shown with “RP” and the runway numbers; they are not shown at airports with full-time towers.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-3 “Traffic Patterns”

notes.front: At what height do propeller-driven aircraft normally fly the traffic pattern?
notes.back: 1,000 feet above ground level, unless the Chart Supplement publishes another altitude.
notes.explanation: Large and turbine aircraft fly it at 1,500 feet AGL or more, and helicopters lower, about 500 feet AGL.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-3 “Traffic Patterns”

notes.front: At what height do large and turbine-powered aircraft enter the traffic pattern?
notes.back: At least 1,500 feet AGL, or 500 feet above the established pattern altitude.
notes.explanation: Propeller aircraft use 1,000 feet AGL; helicopters about 500 feet AGL.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-3 “Traffic Patterns”

notes.front: What is the preferred way for a manned aircraft to enter a non-towered airport’s pattern from the downwind side?
notes.back: On a course 45° to the downwind leg, joining at midfield, at pattern altitude.
notes.explanation: This predictable entry path is airspace a remote pilot should keep clear of near an airport.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: In the traffic pattern, what is the departure?
notes.back: The straight climb out along the runway line after takeoff.
notes.explanation: The AIM’s standard terms are departure, upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-2 “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”

notes.front: In the traffic pattern, what is the upwind leg?
notes.back: A path straight ahead along the extended runway centreline after departure.
notes.explanation: The AIM’s standard terms are departure, upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-2 “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”

notes.front: In the traffic pattern, what is the crosswind leg?
notes.back: A path at right angles to the landing runway, off its takeoff end.
notes.explanation: The AIM’s standard terms are departure, upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-2 “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”

notes.front: In the traffic pattern, what is the downwind leg?
notes.back: A path parallel to the landing runway, flown in the opposite direction to landing.
notes.explanation: The AIM’s standard terms are departure, upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-2 “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”

notes.front: In the traffic pattern, what is the base leg?
notes.back: A path at right angles to the landing runway off its approach end, from downwind to the extended centreline.
notes.explanation: The AIM’s standard terms are departure, upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-2 “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”

notes.front: In the traffic pattern, what is the final approach?
notes.back: A path in the landing direction along the extended runway centreline, from base leg to the runway.
notes.explanation: The AIM’s standard terms are departure, upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-2 “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”

notes.front: Are runway numbers referenced to true north or magnetic north?
notes.back: Magnetic north.
notes.explanation: So runway numbers match a magnetic compass rather than true north.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Runway Markings and Signs”, p. 14-5

notes.front: How is a runway’s number worked out?
notes.back: The whole number nearest one-tenth of the runway centreline’s magnetic direction, measured from the approach direction.
notes.explanation: Parallel runways add L, C or R (left, centre, right).
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Runway Designation Marking”, p. 14-8

notes.front: At a towered airport, may you cross the solid lines of a runway holding position marking without an ATC clearance?
notes.back: No; stop before the solid lines and cross only with an ATC clearance.
notes.explanation: Leaving the runway, you approach the dashed side and need no clearance to cross.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Runway Holding Position Marking”, p. 14-8

notes.front: What colours is a runway holding position sign?
notes.back: White characters outlined in black on a red background.
notes.explanation: It is the airport version of a stop sign and is always paired with the painted holding position marking.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Runway Holding Position Sign”, p. 14-7

notes.front: What does a black runway sign with a white number show?
notes.back: Runway distance remaining, in thousands of feet.
notes.explanation: The last sign, “1”, is at least 950 feet from the runway end.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Runway Distance Remaining Signs”, p. 14-8

notes.front: What may the runway behind a displaced threshold be used for?
notes.back: Takeoffs in either direction, and landings from the opposite direction.
notes.explanation: The threshold marks the beginning of the runway available for landing. A displaced one is marked with white arrows along the centreline and white arrowheads before a white threshold bar.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Displaced Threshold”, p. 14-5; AIM para. 2-3-3 (runway threshold markings)

notes.front: What may the closed part of a runway before a relocated threshold be used for?
notes.back: Taxiing only, not takeoff or landing.
notes.explanation: A relocated threshold, often marked by yellow arrowheads and a white bar, also shortens the opposite-direction runway.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Relocated Runway Threshold”, p. 14-5

notes.front: What airport beacon identifies a civilian land airport?
notes.back: Flashing white and green.
notes.explanation: Beacon colours: white-green land airport; white-yellow water airport; white-yellow-green heliport; two quick whites and a green, military.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Airport Beacon”, p. 14-16

notes.front: What airport beacon identifies a water airport (seaplane base)?
notes.back: Flashing white and yellow.
notes.explanation: Beacon colours: white-green land airport; white-yellow water airport; white-yellow-green heliport; two quick whites and a green, military.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Airport Beacon”, p. 14-16

notes.front: What airport beacon identifies a heliport?
notes.back: Flashing white, yellow and green.
notes.explanation: Beacon colours: white-green land airport; white-yellow water airport; white-yellow-green heliport; two quick whites and a green, military.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Airport Beacon”, p. 14-16

notes.front: What airport beacon identifies a military airport?
notes.back: Two quick white flashes alternating with a green flash.
notes.explanation: Beacon colours: white-green land airport; white-yellow water airport; white-yellow-green heliport; two quick whites and a green, military.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Airport Beacon”, p. 14-16

notes.front: When are airport beacons normally operated?
notes.back: From dusk until dawn (sometimes also in daytime low ceilings or visibility, but that is not required).
notes.explanation: Because daytime use is not required, a pilot must judge the weather for themselves rather than rely on the beacon.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Airport Beacon”, p. 14-16

notes.front: What colour are taxiway edge lights?
notes.back: Blue.
notes.explanation: Some airports also have green taxiway centreline lights.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Taxiway Lights”, p. 14-19

notes.front: What colour are taxiway centreline lights?
notes.back: Green.
notes.explanation: Taxiway edges are blue; centreline lights, where fitted, are green.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Taxiway Lights”, p. 14-19

notes.front: What colours does a VASI use to show the glidepath?
notes.back: Red and white.
notes.explanation: Each light projects white in the upper part of its beam and red in the lower part.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI)”, p. 14-16

notes.front: What glidepath angle does a two-bar VASI normally give?
notes.back: 3 degrees.
notes.explanation: A three-bar VASI gives two glidepaths, the lower normally 3° and the upper ¼° above it.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI)”, p. 14-16

notes.front: How do PAPI (precision approach path indicator) lights differ in layout from a VASI?
notes.back: They are in a single row, normally on the left side of the runway.
notes.explanation: A VASI has its lights in two or three bars.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Other Glidepath Systems”, p. 14-16

notes.front: Is an airport’s secured area always a SIDA?
notes.back: Yes. The air operations area may or may not be a SIDA, but a secured area always is.
notes.explanation: Airports with a SIDA publish a description and map of its boundaries; ask the airport authority if unsure.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 2-3-15 “Security Identification Display Area (SIDA)”

notes.front: What can happen to someone seen entering a SIDA without proper identification?
notes.back: They may be reported to the TSA or airport security and face civil and criminal fines and prosecution.
notes.explanation: Movement into a SIDA is prohibited without authorisation and displayed identification.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 2-3-15 “Security Identification Display Area (SIDA)”

notes.front: Which FAA form is used to report a bird or other wildlife strike?
notes.back: FAA Form 5200-7, Bird/Other Wildlife Strike Report.
notes.explanation: The reports help set standards and document the need for habitat control at airports.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 7-5-3 “Reporting Bird Strikes”

notes.front: You will fly near a non-towered airport. The chart lists no tower, no Flight Service Station and no UNICOM for it. Which frequency should you monitor?
notes.back: MULTICOM, 122.9.
notes.choicesExplained: A: 122.8 is the usual UNICOM frequency, and this airport has no UNICOM. C: 122.7 is also listed as a CTAF/UNICOM frequency (PHAK Fig. 14-1), which this airport lacks.
notes.explanation: With no frequency published for the airport, traffic self-announces on 122.9.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40; Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, Fig. 14-1

notes.front: Monitoring the CTAF, you hear: “Town and Country traffic, Cessna 123 Bravo Foxtrot, left base, runway 18, Town and Country traffic.” Where is that aircraft?
notes.back: On the base leg of a left-hand pattern for runway 18, about to turn onto final.
notes.explanation: Base leg is at right angles to the runway off its approach end; final follows it.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 41

notes.front: You hear: “Town and Country traffic, Cessna 123 Bravo Foxtrot is 10 miles south, inbound for landing.” What should you expect?
notes.back: A manned aircraft approaching from the south that will soon enter the pattern to land.
notes.explanation: The 10-mile call is the first self-announce call; keep scanning to the south and stay clear of the pattern.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: You are flying near a non-towered airport and have heard nothing on the CTAF for 20 minutes. Can you assume no manned aircraft are near?
notes.back: No; radio calls are not mandatory and some aircraft have no radio, so keep scanning.
notes.explanation: The radio is only an extra layer of awareness on top of looking.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 41

notes.front: Your drone is working near a non-towered airport and you see a light aircraft joining downwind. Nothing is wrong. Should you call it on the CTAF to say where you are?
notes.back: No; remote pilots should not transmit on aviation frequencies except in an emergency. Stay clear and give way.
notes.explanation: Remote pilots are not expected to communicate with manned aircraft; they avoid them instead.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 42

notes.front: You hear “Cessna Four-Seven-Two-Kilo-Lima” on the frequency. What is that aircraft’s registration number?
notes.back: N472KL.
notes.explanation: When the make is used in the call sign, the “N” (November) prefix is dropped.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 42

notes.front: How would a pilot say the registration N5GD in full with the phonetic alphabet?
notes.back: “November Five Golf Delta.”
notes.explanation: Letters use their phonetic words; digits are spoken individually.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-7 “Phonetic Alphabet”

notes.front: You have ATC authorisation to fly near a towered airport. Which frequency is most useful to monitor to learn where manned traffic is going?
notes.back: The tower frequency.
notes.explanation: Manned pilots there must keep two-way radio contact with the tower, so their instructions are heard on its frequency.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Towered Airport”, p. 14-2

notes.front: You plan to fly at 300 feet AGL about a mile from a small airport used by light propeller aircraft. At what height will traffic in the pattern normally be flying?
notes.back: About 1,000 feet AGL, and lower as they descend to land.
notes.explanation: Pattern altitude for propeller aircraft is 1,000 feet AGL; the descent towards the runway brings them lower near its ends.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-3 “Traffic Patterns”

notes.front: A runway’s centreline points 184° magnetic from its approach end. What number is painted on that end?
notes.explanation: One-tenth of 184 is 18.4, and the nearest whole number is 18.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Runway Designation Marking”, p. 14-8

notes.front: Tomorrow you will fly two miles from an unfamiliar airport. Where would you check today for temporary runway closures or construction there?
notes.back: The NOTAMs for that airport.
notes.explanation: NOTAMs carry time-critical, temporary information such as runway and taxiway closures and construction.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 67

notes.front: The Chart Supplement lists a non-towered airport’s UNICOM, 123.0, as its CTAF. Which frequency should you monitor when flying nearby?
notes.back: 123.0, the published UNICOM/CTAF, not the usual 122.8.
notes.explanation: UNICOM is usually 122.8, but the published frequency always wins.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: At dusk you see a beacon ahead flashing white, then yellow. What kind of airport is it?
notes.back: A water airport (seaplane base).
notes.choices:
A) Civilian land airport
B) Water airport
C) Heliport
notes.choicesExplained: A: a land airport flashes white and green. C: a heliport flashes white, yellow and green.
notes.explanation: White-yellow is water; white-green is a land airport; white-yellow-green is a heliport.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Airport Beacon”, p. 14-16

notes.front: A beacon shows two quick white flashes, then a green flash, repeating. What kind of airport is it?
notes.back: A military airport.
notes.explanation: The double white flash between greens distinguishes military airports from civilian land airports.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Airport Beacon”, p. 14-16

notes.front: A beacon flashes white, yellow and green in turn. What does it mark?
notes.back: A heliport.
notes.explanation: Three colours means heliport; white-green is a land airport, white-yellow a water airport.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Airport Beacon”, p. 14-16

notes.front: A farm strip is marked “private use, prior permission only” and is not open to the public. Which type of airport is it?
notes.back: A private airport.
notes.explanation: Private airports are for private or restricted use only; civil airports are open to the public.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: Hired to film at an airport, you are asked to walk to a ramp area whose signs say a displayed badge is required. What is this area, and what do you need?
notes.back: A SIDA; you need authorisation and properly displayed identification before entering.
notes.explanation: SIDA badges are issued under 49 CFR part 1542.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 2-3-15 “Security Identification Display Area (SIDA)”

notes.front: A bird strikes a manned aircraft near the airport where you are working, and you are asked how it should be reported. What form applies?
notes.back: FAA Form 5200-7, Bird/Other Wildlife Strike Report.
notes.explanation: Pilots are urged to report every bird or wildlife strike on that form.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 7-5-3 “Reporting Bird Strikes”

notes.front: Your planned survey area includes a hospital helipad. Should you treat it as an airport in your planning?
notes.back: Yes; heliports are airports, so expect helicopters landing and taking off there.
notes.explanation: The airport definition covers any land or water area used for landing or takeoff, including heliports.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: At a non-towered airport with no “RP” marked for runway 27, on which side of the runway will aircraft landing on 27 fly downwind?
notes.back: On the left side of the runway as seen by a landing pilot (a left-hand pattern).
notes.explanation: Turns are to the left unless a right pattern is indicated.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-3 “Traffic Patterns”

notes.front: An aircraft is flying parallel to the runway, in the opposite direction to landing. Which leg is it on?
notes.back: The downwind leg.
notes.explanation: Crosswind and base are at right angles to the runway; upwind and final are along it.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-3-2 “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”

notes.front: A pilot reports “two thousand five hundred” on the frequency. What altitude is that?
notes.back: 2,500 feet.
notes.explanation: Below 18,000 feet MSL, thousands and hundreds are spoken out.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (online edition), 4-2-9 “Altitudes and Flight Levels”

notes.front: Filming from the apron, you see a taxiing aircraft stop just before four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, with the solid lines on its side. Why did it stop there?
notes.back: It is a runway holding position; aircraft do not cross the solid lines towards the runway without clearance.
notes.explanation: The solid lines face the taxiway side; the dashed lines face the runway side.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Runway Holding Position Marking”, p. 14-8

notes.front: What is the difference between a CTAF and UNICOM?
notes.back: CTAF is the role (the common advisory frequency); UNICOM is a kind of ground station whose frequency may serve as the CTAF.
notes.explanation: A CTAF may also be a MULTICOM, Flight Service Station or tower frequency.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 11, p. 65

notes.front: UNICOM or MULTICOM: which has someone on the ground who may answer?
notes.back: UNICOM (a ground station); on MULTICOM, 122.9, pilots only self-announce.
notes.explanation: MULTICOM is used where there is no tower, Flight Service Station or UNICOM.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 7, p. 40

notes.front: Towered versus non-towered airport: where is two-way radio contact required?
notes.back: At a towered airport (with ATC); at a non-towered airport it is not required.
notes.explanation: At a non-towered airport, pilots coordinate by self-announcing on the CTAF.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Towered Airport; Nontowered Airport”, p. 14-2

notes.front: Displaced versus relocated threshold: in which is the runway behind it usable for takeoff?
notes.back: Displaced; behind a relocated threshold the closed part is for taxiing only.
notes.explanation: Displaced thresholds use white arrows; relocated thresholds use yellow arrowheads.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Relocated Runway Threshold; Displaced Threshold”, p. 14-5

notes.front: VASI versus PAPI: which has its lights in a single row?
notes.back: PAPI (normally on the left of the runway); a VASI has two or three bars.
notes.explanation: Both use red and white to show the glidepath.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Other Glidepath Systems”, p. 14-16

notes.front: Taxiway edge lights versus taxiway centreline lights: which are blue?
notes.back: Edge lights are blue; centreline lights are green.
notes.explanation: Both help pilots find their way round the airport at night.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 14, “Taxiway Lights”, p. 14-19
